newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BP roars ahead on Q2 profits, buy back.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BP roars ahead on Q2 profits, buy back.

text.p: Shares in British Petroleum raced nearly five percent ahead on Tuesday to hit a record high, fuelled by bumper second-quarter profits and news of imminent share buy-backs.
Upbeat comments from Chief Executive John Browne, who promised profit would grow over 10 percent this year, further boosted investors' spirits.
Analysts upgraded their forecasts for BP after the oil giant reported a 16 percent rise in second quarter profits despite weaker oil prices.
Better downstream and chemicals results lifted profits to 740 million pounds ($1.2 billion) from 648 million, widely exceeding market forecasts.
The company raised its interim dividend by 10 percent to 5.5 pence per share.
At the close, BP shares stood up 40-1/2 at 862-1/2, just half a penny under its record high of 863 hit earlier on Tuesday.
Browne said analysts had underestimated BP's capability to raise volumes and reduce costs, which contributed about three quarters of BP's progress.
"It's all down to 'self-help'," Browne said after a news conference.
BP set a new 'self-help' target of $500 million for 1997 after the previous $300 million objective was achieved at the half-year stage.

The company plans to buy back some $500 million worth of shares before the 1998 annual shareholders meeting. The oil company will then seek approval for a broader policy to buy-back shares from "time to time".
The buy-backs will be aimed at returning value to shareholders and keeping the growth of issued shares limited.
Browne said the number of share dividend alternatives to cash had increased to 60 percent from 30 percent due to proposed changes to dividend tax credits by Britain's new Labour government.
However pleasing, the share buy-back came as no major surprise to analysts, who were far more impressed with BP's profit growth.
The latest set of results put BP way ahead of other oil majors in terms of return on capital employed (ROCE), analyst John Toalster at SocGen said.
He put BP's ROCE at 18 percent against 12.5 percent for Shell, 13.2 percent for Mobil, and 15.9 percent for Exxon Corp. "There is a wide gap now with the other majors," Toalster said.
BP's refining and marketing profits represented the best second-quarter performance in a decade and results in the chemicals sector rose 24 percent.

Oil and gas production profits were hit by the pound's strength. But the upstream results were unchanged in dollar terms with an improved operating performance offsetting the negative impact of a lower oil price.

BP expects upstream production to rise by over five percent per annum in the next three years. It sees oil demand staying strong, but added that increasing Iraqi exports "may lead to short term price volatility".

Refining margins fell in July and will likely remain under pressure, but there should be compensating effects both from existing marketing activities and recent entry into new markets, BP said, without giving details.
The European downstream merger with Mobil Corp will lead to significantly extra revenues and cost savings later this year.
Chemical prices are expected to remain steady in the short term, but they could weaken later as new capacity comes onstream, BP said. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
